summary: Defines additional elliptic curve groups, based on modular arithmetic over prime fields, for use in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE and IKEv2). It was replaced by RFC 5903.

eli5.summary: When two computers agree on a secret key, they use a math puzzle. This note adds new puzzles based on curved shapes, which are small and hard to crack. It was later replaced.

subtitle: Three elliptic curve groups for secure key exchange in IKE and IKEv2.

tldr.problem: IKE and IKEv2 needed additional elliptic curve groups based on modular arithmetic that align with international standards and offer better software efficiency than binary field curves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three elliptic curve groups over prime fields: 256-bit, 384-bit, and 521-bit, with specified curve parameters and generators matching NIST standards.
tldr.outcome: These groups are now recommended for use in IKE and IKEv2 implementations and align with international cryptographic standards, providing efficient and secure key exchange options.

today: RFC 4753 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 5903, which provides updated ECP groups for IKE and IKEv2.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Groups for Key Exchange
sections.content:
IKE and IKEv2 protocols use Diffie-Hellman groups to allow two parties to establish a shared secret key over an untrusted network. Previously, IKE supported elliptic curve groups over binary fields (GF[2^N]), but these groups use binary arithmetic, which is less efficient in software on conventional processors.

This RFC adds three new elliptic curve groups based on modular arithmetic over prime fields (ECP groups). These curves are defined over integers modulo a large prime p, making them faster to implement in software and aligning IKE with standards from NIST, ISO, ANSI, and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (SECG). The three new groups offer security equivalent to 128-bit, 192-bit, and 256-bit symmetric keys, respectively.
sections.eli5: Two computers can agree on a secret by solving a math puzzle based on a special curve. Using curves over regular numbers instead of binary is faster on normal computers, and everyone uses the same standards now.

sections.title: The Three Elliptic Curve Groups
sections.content:
Each curve is defined by the equation y^2 = x^3 - 3x + b over a prime field. The RFC specifies the prime p, the curve coefficient b, the group order (the number of points on the curve), and a generator point g that serves as the base for the key exchange.

The 256-bit group uses a generalized Mersenne prime of 256 bits and provides 128-bit equivalent security. The 384-bit group uses a similar structure with a 384-bit prime and provides 192-bit equivalent security. The 521-bit group uses the Mersenne prime 2^521 - 1 and provides 256-bit equivalent security. All three curves were chosen verifiably at random using SHA-1 as specified in IEEE standards, ensuring they were not deliberately weakened.
sections.eli5: Each curve lives on a mathematical field defined by a huge prime number. The three sizes are 256, 384, and 521 bits, and they provide the security of 128, 192, and 256-bit encryption keys.

sections.title: Using ECP Groups in Key Exchange
sections.content:
In an IKE or IKEv2 key exchange, each party selects a random private key and computes their public key by multiplying the generator point g by the private key (scalar multiplication on the elliptic curve). The two parties exchange public keys, then each computes the shared secret by multiplying the peer's public key by their own private key, arriving at the same point on the curve.

The Diffie-Hellman public value consists of two components: the x and y coordinates of the elliptic curve point. Each coordinate is padded to the full bit length of the field (256, 384, or 528 bits for the 521-bit group), then concatenated to form the public value. This shared secret point is used in the IKEv2 key derivation to create the actual encryption keys.
sections.eli5: Each computer picks a secret number, does special math with it to get a public number, and swaps public numbers. Then they each do more math to reach the same secret that only they know.

sections.title: Alignment with International Standards
sections.content:
These three ECP groups match elliptic curves standardized by major cryptographic organizations. The 256-bit group is NIST P-256, ISO P-256, and SECG secp256r1. The 384-bit group is NIST P-384 and SECG secp384r1. The 521-bit group is NIST P-521 and SECG secp521r1. Having consistent curve parameters across NIST, ISO, ANSI, and SECG standards reduces implementation errors and allows optimizations and precomputation, resulting in faster and more reliable deployments.

The curves provide security compatible with the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), with the 256-bit group matching AES-128, the 384-bit group matching AES-192, and the 521-bit group matching AES-256. This makes it easy for implementers to choose elliptic curve sizes that match their symmetric encryption algorithms.
sections.eli5: Governments, international organizations, and industry groups all agreed to use the exact same curves. This means every implementation works the same way, and everyone can reuse the same secure math libraries.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
The security of elliptic curve key exchange depends on the difficulty of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem: given a point on the curve, it is computationally infeasible to find the private key that generated it. The RFC notes that all security considerations from IKE and IKEv2 apply here as well, including protection against replay attacks and man-in-the-middle attacks.

The three groups correspond to symmetric key strengths of 128 bits, 192 bits, and 256 bits, respectively. Implementations should choose a curve size appropriate to their security requirements and the strength of other algorithms in use. The test vectors in the RFC allow implementers to verify that their elliptic curve scalar multiplication and key exchange implementations are correct.
sections.eli5: It is so hard to work backwards from the public number to the secret number that no known shortcut exists. The three group sizes match the strength of common encryption keys.
